items.title: Inside the spy plot around Nvidia’s CEO
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,617 new readers. Nvidia’s chips are at the center of the U.S.-China AI race, and Washington has spent years trying to keep the best ones out of Beijing’s hands.

Now, a New York Times report says U.S. intelligence found that an alleged Chinese asset had built close ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang… and the White House chose not to act.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Report: Nvidia CEO targeted by alleged Chinese spy

  • Rowan’s Corner: ‘Sent from my agent’

  • Make ElevenLabs voiceovers sound more natural

  • Anthropic’s AI now monitors its own conversations

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

NVIDIA

🕵️ Report: Nvidia CEO targeted by alleged Chinese spy

Image source: Net Thunder on LinkedIn

The Rundown: The NYT just reported that U.S. officials found Alice Huang, an exec at Singapore-based data center firm Megaspeed, was allegedly passing intelligence to Beijing while keeping close ties with Jensen Huang, with Trump briefed about a year ago.

The details:

  • It’s unclear what Ms. Huang passed to Beijing or its value, but officials worried she could offer insight into Trump’s view on chip sales to China, and into Nvidia itself.

  • Officials didn’t believe Jensen knew of her alleged role when Trump was briefed; he never got a defensive briefing, often given to U.S. citizens targeted by spies.

  • Megaspeed, already under U.S. probe for steering Nvidia chips to China, bought at least $4.8B in Nvidia gear via a sister firm, and remains an Nvidia cloud partner.

  • Nvidia called Jensen’s meetings with Ms. Huang routine, saying customers get ordinary business info and “zero information relevant to national security.”

  • Megaspeed said outside counsel is investigating and it’s cooperating with the U.S., while China called the claims “groundless smears and slanders.”

Why it matters: The report reads like a spy thriller, but nothing has been publicly proven, including whether Ms. Huang passed anything to China. The immediate fallout may hit the loophole allowing firms like Megaspeed to rent Nvidia-powered computing from Southeast Asia to Chinese AI labs — one Trump reopened but may now close.

TOGETHER WITH OPENART

🧑‍🎨 Create a launch video for your business 

The Rundown: Need a launch video for your business? Simply paste your website link, add your brand assets, and define your target audience. OpenArt’s AI video agent will shape the story and messaging while handling the script, motion design, voiceover, and video editing.

With OpenArt, you can:

  • Turn your website, screenshots, or pitch deck into a launch video

  • Create short promos or longer videos to showcase your business

  • Refine scenes, voiceovers, or music by describing the changes

  • Go beyond launches with product ads and UGC-style videos

Create your launch video with OpenArt.

ROWAN’S CORNER

🤖 ‘Sent from my agent’

h/t to @gregisenberg for the tweet

Rowan: “Sent from my agent” is becoming the new “Sent from iPhone.” That’s a tweet my friend Greg Isenberg recently made that’s stirring up conversation.

Basically, “Sent from my iPhone” started as a way to buy forgiveness for typos and messy formatting when emailing someone from your iPhone. But when someone sees “Sent from my agent,” the real message they receive is: you weren’t worth my attention.

There’s real tension here (for me included). Agents are the biggest leverage available right now, and I run several tasks through them, saving me at least a few hours a week. But I also believe going the extra mile and writing something yourself shows the other human respect.

So here’s my line:

  1. Anything that touches a person is me — social posts, messages, recruiting calls, live video.

  2. Anything that’s a task, an agent can do.

I also have a growing thesis that real human relationships will only become more valuable as AI gets better. Anything that risks that trust is probably a bad trade. Personally, if I see “sent from my agent,” I’m deleting the email.

I’ve written before that AI intuition is the most important skill of this decade, knowing which tasks to hand to AI, and this is the perfect example. Use agents everywhere, except on people.

Are you using agents to respond to your emails, or do you think the human touch shows respect? Let me know in the poll at the bottom of the email. I’m curious!

AI TRAINING

🎙️ Make ElevenLabs voiceovers sound more natural

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll add Audio Tags to a short Eleven v4 voiceover, compare it with the plain version, and create a short scene with two speakers.

Step-by-step:

  1. Open ElevenLabs Text to Speech, choose one voice, and select Eleven v4. Generate the guide’s plain script and save it for comparison

  2. Paste the tagged version without changing the spoken words. Keep the same voice and settings so you can hear the difference

  3. Compare the opening, pace, and final line. If the delivery stays flat, make one cue more specific. Change one thing at a time

  4. If a tag gets read aloud, check the model and square brackets. Keep the direction short and place it before the words it should affect

  5. Open Dialogue mode, add two voices, and generate the guide’s exchange. Check the words, speakers, and timing before downloading the clips

Pro tip: Save a plain version before adding tags. A more expressive read may still sound less natural. You can find our full cheat sheet, annotated scripts, and review checklist here.

PRESENTED BY GLEAN

🚀 From data to decisions, faster

The Rundown: Business data spans across apps, warehouses, and BI platforms, while the context behind the numbers lives in documents, tickets, and conversations. Glean’s upcoming webinar helps you bring it all together, find trusted answers, and make data-driven decisions without SQL or a BI background.

In this webinar, you’ll learn how to:

  • Query business data in natural language

  • Quickly build dashboards to track key metrics

  • Connect metrics with enterprise context

Register for the webinar and put AI to work.

ANTHROPIC / AI SAFETY

🚨 Anthropic’s AI now monitors its own conversations

Image source: Anthropic

The Rundown: Anthropic introduced “self-assessment,” a technique where Claude reviews the chat after each reply and flags potential misuse, saying the system has been active since June and catching large-scale abuse that might otherwise be missed.

The details:

  • Claude gives each conversation a quick safety verdict (whether it’s harmful, what kind of harm, and how urgent), which helps prioritize cases for human review.

  • On Claude Fable 5, it catches 78% of potentially harmful conversations flagged by a stronger classifier, and 94% of high-priority ones, at a 1% false-positive rate.

  • It helped uncover 100K+ child-abuse flags from a single API customer, reported to authorities, plus an automated romance-scam operation run through Claude Code.

  • Anthropic admits it’s weak as a lone blocker, cutting attack success in red-team tests only from 79% to 54%, though it made each successful attack cost ~4x more.

Why it matters: After Anthropic’s own reports showed Claude being misused for cyberattacks and weapons work, letting the AI check and flag misuse in its own chats is a welcome layer. Claude brings everything it understands to each judgment, but it can also share the same blind spots, meaning the system isn’t foolproof (yet!).

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Michael used Claude Cowork to build a 3D home design app

Today’s workflow comes from reader Michael Saif:

“I built this web app for a friend who is building a house. It lets you see the finished version of every room in the planned home before anything is built. I described the idea to Claude Cowork, had a short back-and-forth answering its questions, and it built the app in four stages. You can upload one or more floor plans, select a room, and view it from several rotatable 3D angles.

You can then describe how you want the room to look when completed, such as ‘Show me with a dark-colored wood floor with blue walls,’ and ask for changes, like light-colored wood floors. You can also add furniture to see how the room will look when finished, save multiple designs for each room, and export any image as a PNG. The whole build took less than an hour from start to finish.”

items.title: Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon tops the charts (for now)
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,742 new readers. Google spent much of 2026 playing catch-up in the AI race. A month and two frontier models later, it’s sitting at the top of the charts again, sort of.

Gemini 4 Carbon has the numbers to back up all the comeback talk, but like Argon at launch, the public can’t use it yet — and with OpenAI and Anthropic shipping at a similar pace, the crown might not last long.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Google’s Carbon takes the benchmark crown (for now)

  • Nate’s Notebook: Hire a dispatcher first

  • Turn a prompt into a poster with Canva Craft

  • An Anthropic manager bets on junior engineers

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

GOOGLE

💎 Google’s Carbon takes the benchmark crown (for now)

Image source: Google

The Rundown: Google just unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon, a new frontier model built for cybersecurity and long-running coding work that tops 15 of 17 benchmarks on Google’s charts, but isn’t yet public — with only select cyber defenders gaining access to start.

The details:

  • Carbon’s 59 on Artificial Analysis’ “Intelligence Index” takes the top spot from Claude Opus 5.5 and improves 9 points over Google’s Argon from four weeks ago.

  • Carbon’s widest wins over OpenAI’s Astra and Opus came on long-input reasoning (+24 points), hacking (+12), workflow automation (+11), and math (+8).

  • Carbon’s $2/$10 intro API price (per million tokens in/out) is half of Opus 5.5’s and 1/5 of Astra’s, though it doubles to Opus’s rate after the initial discount.

  • Google hasn’t given a date for wider access to Carbon, with Argon previously rolling out around two weeks after its debut to cyber defenders.

Why it matters: Two big models in weeks is a big statement from a Google that spent much of 2026 playing catch-up, and Carbon’s numbers back it up. But nobody outside select cyber defenders can vibe-check those numbers yet, and at the pace OpenAI and Anthropic are shipping, the rankings could change well before Carbon goes public.

TOGETHER WITH GARTNER

📖 AI activity isn't the same as value  

The Rundown: 86% of CIOs say AI risk is growing faster than value — four times faster, on average. These Gartner IT Symposium/Xpo takeaways show CIOs how to compound value, not just activity, and govern AI before risk erodes advantage.

Learn how to:

  • Balance AI value and risk

  • Govern AI through an AI central bank

  • Fill AI safety gaps with human oversight

Download the insights.

NATE’S NOTEBOOK

☕ Nate’s Notebook: Hire a dispatcher first

The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.

Nate: Most mornings, I brain dump my project list into my phone while I wait for coffee. Dot splits that one voice dump into separate chats running at once, each in its own context window. By the time I’m back at my desk, they’re gathering context, doing research, and drafting outlines.

That’s the difference between the agents landing right now. Grok Bot and OpenClaw are monothreads: one worker running unattended. Even with careful rules and profiles, I’ve never been super impressed with that work. Dot is a delegator, handing discrete jobs to threads I can still coach.

Unattended is the hard part. Think about hiring a new assistant: we all underestimate how hard it is for anyone, human or agent, to anticipate what matters to you. Agents will get there, but it takes time and a lot more context. Until then, I stay in the loop for chunking, quality, and coaching.

Last week, I laid out my ladder: read, then write, then send. If you’re not ready for write access, that’s okay. Dot sorts the noise in my inbox and flags what needs me, with no access to write anything. Just letting it read and triage is a smart, useful, powerful first step, and it’s why I’m even more excited to finally get Anthropic’s Duet.

No Dot yet? The brain dump works in a new ChatGPT voice chat, too.

We’re currently in the messy middle. Triage and delegation are worth jumping into now; figure out the rest along the way.

AI TRAINING

🎨 Turn a prompt into a poster with Canva Craft

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll try Canva’s new image model on a workshop poster. You’ll check the headline, add event details you can edit, and make a square version without rebuilding the whole artwork.

Step-by-step:

  1. Open Dream Lab from Canva’s homepage and select Craft. Choose a portrait layout and check your AI allowance before generating

  2. Paste the guide’s brief. Ask for a clear headline and blank space for the event details. Then, check the headline very closely

  3. If the issue remains after one revision, generate the artwork without text and add the heading yourself

  4. Open the image in Canva and add the date, time, and venue as text boxes. Try Magic Layers only if you need to edit words or objects inside the generated image

  5. Make a square version and change the event date in both designs. Check the downloaded files for spelling, cropping, and the correct details

Pro tip: Keep details that may change in ordinary text boxes. A new date should not require another image generation. You can find our full guide, test resources, and prompts here.

PRESENTED BY ENEY BY MACPAW

💬 Just ask. Skip to done.

The Rundown: Eney by MacPaw is a proactive AI assistant that takes tedious work and life tasks off your list on Mac and iPhone. It spots what needs attention and handles tasks with your go-ahead.

With Eney, you can:

  • Act on what’s on your screen with Eney Wand

  • Delegate tasks, big and small

  • Work seamlessly across your favorite apps

Get started with Eney.

AI & THE WORKFORCE

🤝 An Anthropic manager bets on junior engineers

Image source: Felix Rieseberg / J. M. W. Turner

The Rundown: Anthropic engineering manager Felix Rieseberg wrote that he’s dropped the coding interview from his team’s hiring, saying Claude now outperforms people on the short coding tests it relied on — while also offering an optimistic counter-take that AI is letting junior engineers overtake veterans.

The details:

  • Rieseberg, who has led engineering on Claude Code Desktop, says he has seen newer engineers “fly past” likely better coders, and that “hunger beats tenure.”

  • His advice to juniors is to tie one bold idea to higher-ups’ goals and build it as a weekend prototype, since with AI “execution isn’t expensive anymore.”

  • He used Claude Code’s desktop app as an example, with two newer employees prototyping it in one weekend before it went public just over a week later.

Why it matters: A lot of this year’s talk about junior engineers has been gloomy, with Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark saying earlier that AI makes their value “a bit more dubious.” Rieseberg’s taking the opposite stance from inside the same company, with a vote of confidence in agency and AI-enabled ambition over years of experience.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Mario built an AI prospector that pitches websites to local shops

Today’s workflow comes from reader Mario Mitchell:

“I built a set of agents that run every day to find local businesses with no website, build a site for a selected business, and email the mockup to that lead. It’s for anyone who sells web services to local businesses and wants to automate the prospecting.

Each day, my Gemini and ChatGPT agents check the major cities in the state I select, for the industry I select, and find the best businesses that don’t have a website. They add those businesses to a spreadsheet. A second agent reads the spreadsheet, selects the best prospect based on its need for web services and likelihood of buying, and starts building its website.

That agent checks the business’s social media for images and its Google Business Profile for information. It also looks for a logo. If there isn’t one, it creates a logo for them. A third agent takes the mockup and sends an email with it to the lead. A fourth agent is set up to reply once the lead responds, book them on a call, and put the call on the calendar.”

See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

  • 💬 Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe - Nvidia’s AI that transcribes 40 languages

  • 🔴 ChatGPT Dot - OpenAI’s always-on agent, now available via text message

📰 Everything else in AI today

OpenAI is pulling hundreds of staffers into a “war room” for next week’s U.S. midterm elections, hunting for ChatGPT misuse after flagging Russian and Iranian influence campaigns on its models this month.

Artificial Analysis released v5 of its “Intelligence Index” AI leaderboard, now relying more on private tests, with Chinese open models falling further behind in the rankings and OpenAI’s new Terra model outperforming despite its mid-tier level.

New AI startup Particle released Particle-1, a DeepSeek V4.1 Flash variant trained to reason less on coding tasks, using ~45% fewer tokens with near-identical accuracy.

items.title: Google’s AI worlds can now talk back
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,193 new readers. Last year, Genie 3 let you wander an AI-generated world for a few minutes. Genie 4 lets you talk to the ‘people’ living in the simulation.

Google DeepMind’s newest world model brings its own soundtrack too, and a demo of a humanoid robot playing checkers inside one of its worlds shows where Google wants to take things next.

Reminder: Our next live workshop is today at 2 PM EDT — join and learn why AI deep research has gotten worse over the past six months, and how to get sharp, decision-ready reports out of it again. RSVP here.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Genie 4 brings sound and interactivity to AI worlds

  • Anthropic starts developing its own drugs

  • Make editable product mockups with GPT-6.1 Terra

  • Axiom’s AI swarm checks math’s longest proof

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

GOOGLE DEEPMIND

🧞 Genie 4 brings sound and interactivity to AI worlds

Image Source: Google DeepMind

The Rundown: Google DeepMind just introduced Genie 4, its next-gen world model that turns prompts into explorable, photorealistic scenes in real time, with features like built-in, natively generated audio and lifelike people that users can actually interact with.

The details:

  • Genie 4 is the first Genie model to generate its own sound, like background noise and music, with characters in the worlds also now able to hold live conversations.

  • Users move with keyboard controls and can use text prompts to create changes mid-scene, with the scene staying coherent between inputs.

  • A simulated Apptronik Apollo robot played checkers in one demo, with Gemini 4 Argon planning each move in a nod to Genie’s future robot-training applications.

  • The model debuts in research preview for trusted testers, with Google’s AI Ultra subscribers and Gemini API partners getting access next.

Why it matters: Genie’s progress has been pretty wild to watch, and this iteration’s jump, with sound and characters you can actually talk to, takes it somewhere new. The gaming applications are obvious, but Genie is starting to look as much like a full-blown director’s tool as a world simulator.

TOGETHER WITH CUBE

🧠 The semantic layer for AI

The Rundown: Cube is the semantic layer for AI. Every agent gets the same governed answer from your metric definitions and access rules. Ask the hardest questions, get real answers.

With Cube, you can:

  • Connect Snowflake, Databricks, or BigQuery

  • Let AI build and maintain your data model

  • See how Brex reached nearly 90% answer relevance

Try Cube free (no card needed).

ANTHROPIC

💊 Anthropic starts developing its own drugs

Image source: Anthropic

The Rundown: Anthropic shared early results with its drug-development partners and revealed it’s now running its own drug discovery programs, including buying Mithril Medicine, a solo-founder biotech whose Claude-assisted muscular dystrophy candidate could reach human trials as early as late 2028.

The details:

  • The candidate showed promise in mice within 18 months, with Claude helping solo founder Cody Tranbarger juggle contracts and tests at 11 outside labs.

  • Tranbarger also turned out to be “Professor Oak,” a biotech account run pseudonymously on X for six years, and calls the setup a “Pipeline-in-a-Person.”

  • At Enveda, Claude wrote a first draft of a key regulatory filing in 4 hours vs. ~3 months by hand, and also flagged seven batch-record issues humans missed.

  • In another case, three of roughly 35K antibodies Claude designed for Divergence Labs appeared to beat today’s main drug at unhooking allergy triggers from cells.

  • This week’s IPO filing pitched a global pharma market expected to top $2T this year, but Anthropic warned its own drug bets “may never generate revenue.”

Why it matters: Dario Amodei said in August to expect “early glimmers” from Anthropic’s biology push in the coming months, and we’re seeing the groundwork for that. With Anthropic also running its own wet lab, and its IPO filing saying Claude can operate gear like microscopes, the pieces for AI’s hands-on science are falling into place fast.

AI TRAINING

📦 Make editable product mockups with GPT-6.1 Terra

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use the new GPT-6.1 Terra to build a product mockup in Blender. You’ll create two color options and a wide campaign image, then save the scene so you can handle client changes without starting over.

Step-by-step:

  1. Save an empty Blender project and connect Terra through ChatGPT Work’s Computer Use plugin. Keep its access limited to your practice project

  2. Give Terra the guide’s carton dimensions and colors. Check the size, then add the product name and label as editable text

  3. Add a camera and studio lights, then render a small preview. Check that the lettering is readable, the edges look right, and the carton sits on the ground

  4. Copy the scene to make a second color option. Create a wide version with the product on the right and space for a headline on the left

  5. Export all three images and reopen the saved Blender file. Check the image sizes and confirm you can still change the text and product colors

Pro tip: Keep the camera and lights fixed when comparing colors. Otherwise, a lighting change can make one option seem better for the wrong reason.

PRESENTED BY SCRIBE

🔍 Consultants take months. Scribe takes days.

The Rundown: Most orgs map workflows the slow way: outside teams, interviews, and months of workshops. Scribe Optimize maps how work happens across your org automatically.

With Scribe Optimize, you can:

  • Map real workflows — no surveys or consultants

  • Surface inefficiencies leadership can’t currently see

  • Build your AI strategy on ground truth, not gut feel

See what's actually happening in your org.

AI & MATH

🧮 Axiom’s AI swarm checks math’s longest proof

Image source: Axiom

The Rundown: AI math startup Axiom completed a fully machine-checked version of math’s longest-ever proof, called the ‘Classification of Finite Simple Groups’, with its team steering an AI agent swarm that rebuilt the decades-long effort in 24 days.

The details:

  • The theorem catalogs what Axiom calls the “periodic table of symmetry,” a full list of the basic pieces that every symmetry pattern in math breaks down into.

  • 100+ mathematicians spread the original across roughly 15K pages and 500+ papers, and Axiom says no single expert has read it cover to cover.

  • Axiom broke the work into 108 milestones, then dozens of agents produced ~43M lines of Lean, the coding language that lets a computer verify each logical step.

  • The theorem stands, but AI caught a false claim in one key step, then patched it with a new proof based on 1976 work by mathematician Ronald Solomon.

Why it matters: OpenAI used agents to crack the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem in September, and now a startup has pointed one at a 15K-page proof that no mathematician could check alone. Dario Amodei’s “country of geniuses in a datacenter” feels like it’s coming to life in the sciences, and a lot more progress is coming with it.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Anuradha built a one-person sales team with Claude

Today’s workflow comes from reader Anuradha:

“I use Claude, connected live to Airtable through MCP, as a one-person GTM team. It runs a daily pipeline war room, drafts outreach, and helps me create data-driven LinkedIn content.

I start a morning war room session by opening Claude and letting it read my live Airtable pipeline. It gives me a scoreboard of what moved, what is stuck, and who needs a touch that day. It drafts outreach using a written style rulebook: peer tone, hypothesis framing, short sentences, and no brochure language. I review everything and send it myself.

I log every LinkedIn post in Airtable with its full text, followed by its analytics: impressions, industry mix, seniority, comments, and notes on what worked. Before writing a new post, Claude reviews the full post history, ranks the posts, and identifies which patterns drove reach and engagement from my target audience. What makes this work is that the analytics live in the same table as the content, so every post makes the next one smarter.”

items.title: The AI bubble meets Anthropic’s real numbers
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,851 new readers. The AI race in 2026 has been about more than just the best models… It’s also been about which top U.S. lab reaches Wall Street first. While OpenAI has backed off in that arena, Anthropic just opened the books with its official IPO filing.

What’s inside isn’t what many of the “AI bubble” critics predicted — a business growing far faster than it spends, and in typical Anthropic fashion, still openly voicing its concerns about what it’s building.

P.S. — Want a chance to be featured in The Rundown? Give GPT-6.1 Terra one real task this week and share how it went in the Workflow Hub by Friday, Oct. 30.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Anthropic officially files to go public

  • OpenAI’s next batch of AI science discoveries arrives

  • Turn sales call notes into follow-up emails with AI

  • OpenAI’s new Terra cuts the cost of AI computer use

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

ANTHROPIC

💰 Anthropic officially files to go public

Image source: SEC.gov

The Rundown: Anthropic just filed its S-1 for a Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT, giving investors a look at its finances, a unique ownership setup designed around its safety mission, and the risks it says come with building more capable AI.

The details:

  • Revenue hit $16.3B in the first six months of 2026, about 14x from a year earlier, and the June quarter alone turned a $974M operating profit.

  • Anthropic has raised $141B to date but still holds about $132B of it, meaning it has spent a net of roughly $9.4B to build a business that makes $11.6B a quarter.

  • All seven co-founders pledged 80% of their stakes to charity, and the board can give its Public Benefit Fund up to 2% more shares per 50% stock climb.

  • Claude wrote over 90% of Anthropic’s code in September, and staff’s Claude use, valued at retail prices, first passed monthly cash payroll in April.

  • A safety area of the filing also warned that some internal work run by Claude could grow “difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control.”

Why it matters: One of the loudest knocks on the AI boom was that the frontier labs’ businesses wouldn’t hold up. Anthropic just answered that with a profitable June quarter and nearly all the money it raised still in the bank. The debate now moves from whether the business works to what it’s actually worth, with ANT’s opening valuation still awaited.

OPENAI & SCIENTIFIC DISCOVERY

💡 OpenAI’s next batch of AI science discoveries arrives

Image source: OpenAI / Clay Mathematics Institute

The Rundown: OpenAI said its unreleased models made new discoveries in physics, math, and computer science, including part of a Millennium Prize problem and a disproof of a decades-old computing assumption, weeks after its massive 722-paper math drop.

The details:

  • In computer science, the models disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a decades-old assumption that hundreds of papers rely on.

  • The scientists who first proposed the hypothesis are reviewing the claim, writing that if it holds, “it will change an important part of theoretical computer science.”

  • OAI says its models also proved a 35-year-old wave conjecture and part of a $1M Millennium Prize problem, with Nobel laureate David Gross leading the review.

  • The company says it does “not seek academic credit” for the results, and agreed to release all its raw data on the hypothesis so anyone can check the work.

Why it matters: Where Oct. 6’s math drop was about volume, this one is three results that are each famous on their own, with the main proofs computer-verified before the announcement. The prior release showed AI could churn out research by the hundreds, but today proves it can also crack the problems whole fields are organized around.

AI TRAINING

📞 Turn sales call notes into follow-up emails with AI

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll try Inception’s new Mercury 3 to turn three sales call notes into follow-ups. You’ll check the prices and promises, change one customer’s needs, and compare the result with your usual model.

Step-by-step:

  1. Open OpenRouter Chat and choose Inception’s Mercury 3. Check the usage cost and start a fresh conversation without connected accounts.

  2. Paste the guide’s fictional product facts and three call notes. Ask for a plan recommendation and a short, unsent reply for each lead.

  3. Check every recommendation against the offer. A plan that fits the team size can still miss a required feature, and a requested discount is not an approved one.

  4. Change one lead from eight users to 18. Mercury should withdraw its earlier recommendation because the largest listed plan only covers 15 people.

  5. Try the same task with your usual model. Compare mistakes, waiting, and time spent fixing the drafts before deciding which to keep.

Pro tip: Measure the time to a reply you would actually use. Fast text is less useful when it needs a long edit. You can get our test resources and prompts here.

The Rundown: Should you prompt a Vision Language Model (VLM) or train a specialist to label data? One labeled example boosts defect classification F1 by 25 points, but 10 examples give specialists the edge.

What you’ll learn:

  • Teach VLMs domain-specific labels

  • When training justifies the cost

  • Few-shot prompting with Agentic Labeling

Read the findings and join the workshop with Nebius.

OPENAI

🌎 OpenAI’s new Terra cuts the cost of AI computer use

Image source: OpenAI

The Rundown: OpenAI just released GPT-6.1 Terra, an upgrade to its mid-tier model with a focus on computer use, speed, and efficiency — now live in ChatGPT and OAI’s Codex coding tool at half the API price of the GPT-5.6 version it replaces.

The details:

  • Terra finishes tasks over 3x faster than the pricier Astra and Sol, while tying Astra on computer use and nearly matching both on visual reasoning.

  • In OAI’s own testing, Terra cost roughly 1/9 as much per task as Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, though Opus outscored it where the two were compared.

  • Despite costing half as much as its predecessor, Terra cut its hallucination rate in OAI’s testing from 53.6% to 16.7%, with other gains across the board.

  • OAI rated Terra’s cyber skills as “Critical” on its Preparedness Framework risk scale, and the model ships with the same safeguards built for GPT-6 Astra.

Why it matters: Terra is a solid upgrade that certainly cuts costs for quick, reliable work, but not one that is going to get the buzzy headlines, particularly with Anthropic’s models dominating the leaderboards. Claude’s weekly average token volume on OpenRouter is up 3.6x since Opus 5.5’s debut, and a cheaper mid-tier model is unlikely to change that.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ A Rundown reader built a reading app staffed by Claude Code agents

Today’s workflow comes from an anonymous Rundown reader:

“I wanted a reader for my own PDFs and EPUBs where I could write notes in the margin next to the line they belonged to. Nothing I tried did that well, so I built Helicon, a free reader for iPhone and iPad. I use it every day.

I do not write most of the code by hand. I run several Claude Code sessions, each with one responsibility. A development session builds the app in Swift. A marketing session reads the usage numbers and finds places to tell people about the app. A separate designer agent, which did not draw the screens, chooses between two or three prototype variants before any UI change is built.

The part that made this work is turning every mistake into a check rather than a note. When an agent gets something wrong, we turn the lesson into a test, script, or guard that prevents the same bad step next time.”
